newsitem.title: HUNGARY: KPMG sees east Euro revenues up at $300mln by 2000.
newsitem.headline: KPMG sees east Euro revenues up at $300mln by 2000.

text.p: Accountancy company KPMG said on Monday that it planned to boost its fee revenues from eastern Europe to $300 million by the year 2000 from about $120 million projected for this year.

European Executive Partner Richard J. Ebling told journalists following a regional conference of KPMG partners that the firm also planned to raise the number of its resident full-time employees to 5,000 by 2000 from 2,200.
"This is quite a significant expansion," he said. "In some of the eastern European countries, the market is very strong."
KPMG is present in 19 countries of the region.

KPMG Chairman Colin Sharman added that KPMG wanted to keep its traditional European markets, but also wanted to exploit the increasing opportunities in emerging markets and sees the eastern part of Europe as a good area of potential growth.

He said KPMG's strategy was shifting towards the better utilisation of local human resources in the countries of its operations and it would concentrate on making the flow of information more effective through computer development and traing.
Michael Kevehazi, Chairman of KPMG's Hungarian subsidiary said expansion in the region and the inflow of capital was made hard by under-developed legal structures in some of the countries.
He said the accounting regulations of Hungary and the Czech Republic were the most developed in the region and they were closely followed by Poland and Slovakia.
"Other countries are some years behind and this is demonstrated by the (amount of) investments they attract," he added.

Kevehazi said that Hungary, generating revenues of 2.3 billion forint ($12.3 million) in 1996, the Czech Republic and Poalnd were KPMG's core eastern European markets but Russia, once its modernised its financial system, would offer vast expansion opportunities.
He added that Price Waterhouse and Ernst & Young were KPMG's main competitors in the region.
